A large new study published in Nature Communications reveals that children and adolescents who had COVID-19 face a significantly higher risk of developing heart-related problems in the months following their infection — and this risk applies even to kids who had no pre-existing heart conditions.

Researchers analyzed electronic health records (digital medical files stored by hospitals) from 19 children's hospitals and health institutions across the United States, collected between March 2020 and September 2023. The study included nearly 298,000 children and teens who tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 (the virus that causes COVID-19) and over 915,000 who tested negative and served as a comparison group. All participants were under 21 years old, with an average age of about 7.75 years.

The team focused on what scientists call "post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2" — or PASC, meaning health problems that appear or linger after the initial infection has cleared. Specifically, they tracked heart-related conditions appearing between 28 and 179 days after infection.

The results were striking. Children who had COVID-19 were significantly more likely than uninfected children to develop a wide range of cardiovascular (heart and blood vessel) problems, including high blood pressure, irregular heartbeats (arrhythmias), inflammation of the heart muscle (myocarditis), heart failure, disease of the heart muscle (cardiomyopathy), cardiac arrest, blood clots (thromboembolism), chest pain, and heart palpitations (the feeling of a racing or fluttering heart).

Overall, children who had COVID-19 were 63% more likely to develop any cardiovascular condition compared to those who had not been infected. The risk of inflammatory heart disease — which includes myocarditis and pericarditis (inflammation of the sac around the heart) — was nearly three times higher in COVID-positive children without pre-existing heart defects.

The study also examined children with congenital heart defects (CHDs) — structural heart problems present from birth, which are the most common birth defect. Children with CHDs who had COVID-19 also showed elevated risks across almost all heart-related outcomes. For example, the risk of myocarditis was nearly four times higher in COVID-positive children with CHDs compared to their uninfected peers.

Importantly, the increased risks were consistent regardless of the child's age, sex, race or ethnicity, weight, or the COVID-19 variant they were infected with. Even children with no prior history of heart problems showed elevated risks after infection.

In terms of absolute numbers, the risks for individual conditions remained relatively low — for instance, chest pain occurred in about 1.23% of COVID-positive children without heart defects compared to 0.61% in uninfected children. However, given how many children have been infected worldwide, even small percentage increases translate to large numbers of affected kids.

The researchers emphasize that awareness of these risks is crucial so that doctors can monitor children after COVID-19 infection, refer them to specialists when needed, and begin treatment early to prevent long-term complications. The findings call for dedicated healthcare resources and long-term heart health monitoring for children who have had COVID-19.

Children Who Had COVID-19 Face Significantly Higher Risk of Heart Problems Afterward

Philadelphia, PA — August 18, 2026

A large new study has found that children and teenagers who were infected with COVID-19 face a significantly higher risk of developing a wide range of heart-related problems in the months after infection compared to those who were never infected. The research, published in Nature Communications, analyzed electronic health records from nearly 1.2 million young patients across 19 children's hospitals and health institutions in the United States, making it one of the largest studies of its kind in the pediatric population.

The study examined health outcomes between 28 and 179 days after a confirmed COVID-19 infection — a period known as the "post-acute" phase, sometimes called Long COVID. Researchers found that COVID-19-positive children and adolescents were at increased risk for conditions including high blood pressure, irregular heartbeats, heart muscle inflammation (myocarditis), heart failure, a weakened heart muscle (cardiomyopathy), cardiac arrest, dangerous blood clots, chest pain, and heart palpitations (a sensation of a racing or fluttering heartbeat), compared to uninfected peers. The overall risk of experiencing any cardiovascular outcome was 2.32% among COVID-19-positive children, compared to 1.38% among uninfected children. Children with pre-existing congenital heart defects — structural heart problems present from birth — showed even higher absolute rates, with 5.57% of COVID-19-positive children with these defects experiencing a cardiovascular outcome, compared to 4.00% of uninfected children with the same defects.

The study drew on records from 297,920 COVID-19-positive individuals and 915,402 COVID-19-negative controls, all under 21 years of age, seen at 19 U.S. children's hospitals between March 2020 and September 2023. Every participant had at least six months of follow-up data. To ensure a fair comparison between the two groups, researchers used a statistical technique called propensity score stratification, which accounts for hundreds of patient characteristics — such as age, race, obesity, and prior health conditions — that could otherwise skew the results. The elevated cardiovascular risks were seen consistently across all age groups, sexes, racial and ethnic backgrounds, and across different COVID-19 virus variants including Delta and Omicron.

Notably, the increased risk was not limited to children already known to have heart problems. The study's authors write that "children and adolescents without a history of any cardiovascular outcomes before SARS-CoV-2 infection showed increased risks, suggesting a broad potential impact on those previously considered at low risk of cardiovascular disease." Heart muscle inflammation (myocarditis) showed some of the sharpest increases in risk: COVID-19-positive children without pre-existing heart defects were nearly 3.66 times more likely to develop myocarditis than uninfected peers. The findings held up through extensive additional testing designed to rule out statistical errors and other explanations.

This research was conducted as part of the NIH RECOVER Initiative — a national program funded by the National Institutes of Health to understand the long-term effects of COVID-19. The study draws on data from nineteen U.S. children's hospitals and health institutions, collectively covering over 30 million patients under the age of 21, including more than 3 million individuals under 21 affected by COVID-19. Participating institutions span a broad geographic and demographic range, representing public and private healthcare systems across 41 states.

COVID-19 is not just an adult problem — and a major new study proves it.

A large study published in Nature Communications analyzed health records from nearly 1.2 million children and teenagers across 19 U.S. hospitals to understand what happens to the heart after a COVID-19 infection. The results are a wake-up call for parents, pediatricians, and policymakers alike.

Key findings:

- Children who had COVID-19 were 63% more likely to develop some form of heart-related condition in the months following infection compared to those who were never infected — whether or not they had a pre-existing heart condition.
- The risk of myocarditis (inflammation of the heart muscle) was nearly 4 times higher in COVID-positive children with a pre-existing heart defect, and nearly 3.7 times higher in those without one.
- Common symptoms like chest pain and heart palpitations (a fluttering or racing heartbeat) were significantly more frequent after infection, with chest pain being nearly twice as likely in infected children without pre-existing heart conditions.

These risks held up across all ages, genders, racial groups, and even across different virus variants like Delta and Omicron.

The study followed 297,920 COVID-positive children and 915,402 uninfected controls, making it one of the largest pediatric studies of its kind.

This research reminds us that "mild" COVID in kids may not always be mild in the long run.

Are we doing enough to monitor children's heart health after COVID-19 infection?

COVID Isn't Just a "Mild Kid's Disease" — New Research Reveals Serious Heart Risks That Linger for Months

When COVID-19 swept the globe, many parents breathed a sigh of relief hearing that children tend to get less sick than adults. And while that's largely true for the acute illness, a major new study is sounding the alarm about what can happen to kids' hearts in the months *after* the infection clears.

**What Did Researchers Study?**

Scientists from the NIH-funded RECOVER Initiative — a national research effort to understand the long-term effects of COVID-19 — examined health records from 19 children's hospitals across the United States. They looked at nearly 300,000 children and teenagers who had tested positive for COVID-19 and compared them to over 900,000 similar kids who had not been infected, tracking their health between 28 and 179 days after their initial test. That window is what researchers call the "post-acute" phase — the weeks and months after the initial infection when long-term complications can emerge.

The study also paid special attention to children with congenital heart defects (CHDs) — meaning heart problems that are present from birth, like holes in the heart or malformed valves. CHDs are the most common type of birth defect, so understanding COVID's impact on this group was a key goal.

**The Findings: A Long Shadow Over Young Hearts**

The results were striking. Children and teenagers who had COVID-19 were significantly more likely to develop a range of heart-related problems in the months following infection compared to those who were never infected.

Across both kids with and without pre-existing heart defects, COVID-19 survivors faced a 63% higher risk of experiencing *any* cardiovascular (heart and blood vessel) complication during the follow-up period. That's not a small number — and it held up across age groups, races, sexes, and even across different COVID variants like Delta and Omicron.

Some of the most concerning individual findings included:
- **Myocarditis** (inflammation of the heart muscle) was nearly 4 times more likely in COVID-positive children with CHDs, and nearly 3.7 times more likely in those without CHDs.
- **Chest pain** was twice as likely in kids with CHDs who had COVID.
- **Palpitations** (the feeling of a racing or fluttering heartbeat) were about twice as common in COVID-positive children.
- **Heart failure**, **cardiomyopathy** (a disease of the heart muscle), and **cardiac arrest** were all significantly elevated.

Even kids who had no history of any heart problems before catching COVID showed increased risks — meaning this isn't just a story about vulnerable children getting sicker. It's about a virus that can affect hearts that were previously perfectly healthy.

**What About Kids With Pre-Existing Heart Conditions?**

Children born with heart defects already face unique health challenges. This study found that COVID-19 raised their risk even further. For example, kids with CHDs who had COVID were 77% more likely to develop heart failure compared to uninfected peers with the same condition. They also faced more than double the risk of chest pain and palpitations.

Interestingly, the overall pattern of risk was similar between children with and without CHDs — COVID raised cardiovascular risk in both groups. However, children with CHDs tended to have higher *absolute* risks (meaning more cases overall), likely because their hearts are already under more strain.

**How Big Was This Study?**

Scale matters in medical research. This study included 297,920 COVID-positive children and 915,402 COVID-negative children — one of the largest pediatric COVID studies ever conducted. The average age of participants was about 7.75 years. The data spanned from March 2020 to September 2023, capturing multiple waves of the pandemic and multiple virus variants.

**Why Does This Matter?**

Many families and even some doctors may assume that once a child recovers from COVID, the danger has passed. This research challenges that assumption. The heart complications identified — some of them serious — were showing up weeks and months after the initial illness, often in children who seemed to have recovered just fine.

The good news is that awareness is the first step to action. Doctors who know about these risks can watch more closely for warning signs, order appropriate tests sooner, and connect families with heart specialists when needed. For children with pre-existing heart conditions, this may mean more proactive check-ins after a COVID diagnosis.

**Key Takeaways for Parents and Caregivers**

- COVID-19 can have lasting effects on children's hearts, even in kids who seemed to recover quickly.
- Symptoms like chest pain, palpitations, or unusual fatigue in the weeks or months after COVID deserve medical attention — don't dismiss them.
- Children with congenital heart defects may need extra monitoring after a COVID infection.
- These risks were found across all ages, races, and sexes studied, and were consistent regardless of which COVID variant caused the infection.
- The findings reinforce the importance of prevention — including vaccination — to protect children from both the acute illness and its potential long-term consequences.

This research is a call to action: for pediatricians to stay vigilant, for parents to stay informed, and for the medical community to continue studying and addressing the long-term impacts of COVID-19 on our youngest patients.

Children and adolescents who have had COVID-19 face a significantly elevated risk of developing cardiovascular complications in the months following infection — and this risk extends even to those with no prior heart history. This large U.S. cohort study, published in Nature Communications, analyzed electronic health records from 19 children's hospitals and health institutions, comparing nearly 298,000 SARS-CoV-2-positive patients under age 21 to over 915,000 uninfected controls, with follow-up focused on the 28- to 179-day post-infection window.

The study found that COVID-19-positive children had meaningfully higher rates of a wide range of cardiovascular outcomes compared to uninfected peers. These included hypertension, ventricular arrhythmias, myocarditis, heart failure, cardiomyopathy, cardiac arrest, thromboembolism, chest pain, and palpitations. Myocarditis was among the most striking findings, occurring at more than three times the rate in COVID-positive children without congenital heart defects (CHDs) compared to uninfected controls.

An important and novel aspect of this study is its focus on children with congenital heart defects — the most common congenital disorder in children. Both CHD and non-CHD groups showed elevated cardiovascular risks after COVID-19 infection. Children with CHDs who tested positive had a heart failure rate of 1.61%, compared to 1.18% in uninfected CHD peers. In children without CHDs, chest pain occurred in 1.23% of COVID-positive patients versus 0.61% in controls. Across the full cohort, 5.57% of COVID-positive children with CHD developed any post-acute cardiovascular outcome, compared to 4.00% of uninfected CHD children; for non-CHD children, the rates were 2.19% versus 1.26%, respectively.

Importantly, elevated risks were consistent regardless of age group, sex, race/ethnicity, obesity status, COVID-19 severity, or which virus variant caused the infection. Even children with no prior cardiovascular history showed increased risk, broadening the population clinicians should monitor. Adolescents aged 12 and older and children aged 5–11 showed higher risks than those under 5. Patients who had severe acute COVID-19 had higher rates of all composite cardiovascular outcomes than those with mild or asymptomatic infection.

For clinical practice, these findings carry clear implications. Clinicians caring for children and adolescents with a history of COVID-19 — particularly in the first six months after infection — should maintain a low threshold for cardiovascular evaluation when patients present with chest pain, palpitations, fatigue, or other suggestive symptoms. Children with CHDs may warrant even closer post-infection follow-up, especially for arrhythmias and heart failure. Referral to pediatric cardiology should be considered when symptoms arise. Immunocompromised children also showed heightened cardiovascular risk regardless of CHD status, representing another group deserving heightened vigilance.

The study's large, diverse, multi-institutional dataset strengthens confidence in these findings. However, clinicians should be aware that diagnoses were based on billing codes without individual chart review, and some mild or home-tested infections may have been missed in the control group. Future research should examine longer-term cardiovascular outcomes and the impact of CHD subtype and surgical repair status on post-COVID risk.

COVID Isn't Just a Respiratory Disease in Kids — And the Heart Pays the Price

You've likely heard that children "do fine" with COVID-19. While it's true that severe acute illness is less common in pediatric patients, a landmark new study published in Nature Communications challenges the idea that kids simply bounce back without lasting consequences — especially when it comes to the heart.

**A Study Built on Real-World Data From Nearly 1.2 Million Children**

Researchers from the NIH RECOVER Initiative analyzed electronic health records from 19 U.S. children's hospitals and health systems, covering patients under 21 seen between March 2020 and September 2023. The cohort included nearly 298,000 SARS-CoV-2-positive children and adolescents, compared against more than 915,000 uninfected controls. Every patient had at least a six-month follow-up after entering the study. This is one of the largest pediatric COVID-19 outcomes studies to date.

The team specifically looked at what happened to the heart in the "post-acute" window — between 28 and 179 days after infection — a period that captures long COVID cardiovascular effects while avoiding the acute phase noise.

**The Findings: A Broad Pattern of Elevated Cardiac Risk**

Across nearly every cardiovascular outcome studied, children who had COVID-19 faced meaningfully higher rates of new diagnoses compared to those who hadn't been infected.

Some of the most striking findings:

- **Myocarditis** (inflammation of the heart muscle) was substantially more common in COVID-positive children without pre-existing heart disease, with an absolute risk of 0.034% versus 0.010% in controls.
- **Chest pain** was nearly twice as common in infected children without congenital heart disease — 1.23% versus 0.61% in uninfected peers.
- **Palpitations** were more than twice as common in COVID-positive children with congenital heart defects (CHDs) compared to uninfected CHD patients.
- **Heart failure** rates were higher in infected children with CHDs — 1.61% versus 1.18% in uninfected CHD controls.
- **Hypertension, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy, cardiac arrest, and thromboembolism** all showed elevated rates in infected children, in both those with and without pre-existing heart conditions.

Looking at the "any cardiovascular outcome" composite: 5.57% of COVID-positive children with CHDs developed at least one new cardiovascular condition, compared to 4.00% of uninfected CHD peers. In children without CHDs, the rates were 2.19% versus 1.26%.

**What About Kids With Congenital Heart Disease?**

This study is the first large-scale analysis to specifically examine how prior COVID-19 infection affects children with CHDs — the most common congenital disorder in children. The findings are reassuring in one sense: the pattern of increased cardiovascular risk after COVID-19 was broadly consistent between children with and without CHDs.

However, children with CHDs who contracted COVID-19 showed a notably higher risk of atrial fibrillation compared to their uninfected CHD counterparts — an arrhythmia that warrants careful monitoring in this already-vulnerable population.

**This Risk Spans All Demographics and Variants**

Importantly, the elevated cardiovascular risk after COVID-19 was consistent regardless of age group, sex, race/ethnicity, obesity status, severity of the acute COVID-19 illness, or which viral variant (pre-Delta, Delta, or Omicron) caused the infection. Even children who had no prior cardiovascular history showed increased risk — meaning this isn't just a story about kids who were already sick.

**What This Means for Your Practice**

These findings carry direct implications for how clinicians approach pediatric post-COVID follow-up:

1. **Don't dismiss cardiac symptoms in post-COVID kids.** Chest pain and palpitations are the most common cardiovascular complaints after COVID-19 in children. When a child presents with these symptoms weeks to months after a COVID-19 diagnosis, take them seriously — even if the child seemed to have a mild infection.

2. **Consider cardiovascular screening for higher-risk patients.** Children with CHDs who have had COVID-19 deserve heightened cardiac surveillance, particularly for arrhythmias. Timely referral to pediatric cardiology may be warranted.

3. **Broaden the surveillance window.** The post-acute cardiovascular risk window extends well beyond the first few weeks. This study tracked outcomes up to 179 days post-infection — clinicians should maintain awareness of potential cardiac complications for months after COVID-19 diagnosis.

4. **Don't assume "mild COVID" means no long-term cardiac risk.** The elevated risk was seen even in children with non-severe acute illness.

**The Bottom Line**

COVID-19 leaves a cardiovascular footprint in children — one that is broader, more varied, and more persistent than many clinicians may realize. With nearly 300,000 pediatric cases in this analysis, the signal is clear: SARS-CoV-2 infection increases the risk of a wide range of heart-related outcomes in children and adolescents, from common symptoms like chest pain to serious conditions like myocarditis, heart failure, and arrhythmias.

As the pandemic recedes from acute emergency status, the long-term cardiovascular health of the millions of children who were infected deserves sustained clinical attention. Timely recognition, appropriate referral, and vigilant follow-up could make a meaningful difference in outcomes for these young patients.

This retrospective cohort study examined post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC) — defined here as new health conditions emerging 28–179 days after infection — with a specific focus on cardiovascular outcomes in children and adolescents, including those with congenital heart defects (CHDs, structural abnormalities of the heart present at birth). Drawing on electronic health records (EHR) from 19 U.S. children's hospitals participating in the NIH RECOVER consortium, the study covered the period March 2020 to September 2023.

The analytic cohort comprised 297,920 SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals and 915,402 SARS-CoV-2-negative controls, all under age 21 with at least six months of follow-up. Among these, 51.4% were male, with a mean age of 7.75 years (SD 6.11). Within the positive group, 13,646 had CHDs and 284,274 did not; the negative group included 46,962 with CHDs and 868,440 without. Outcomes were ascertained using validated ICD and SNOMED diagnostic codes; patients with multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C), Kawasaki disease, or chronic/end-stage kidney disease were excluded.

To address confounding in this observational design, the authors used propensity score stratification across quintiles, incorporating hundreds of covariates — demographics, clinical complexity (via the Pediatric Medical Complexity Algorithm), healthcare utilization, vaccination status, and pandemic timing. Relative risks (RR) were estimated using stratified modified Poisson regression, chosen for its collapsibility properties. Empirical equipoise was confirmed prior to analysis. Negative control outcome experiments (36 outcomes) were used to detect and calibrate residual systematic bias.

The primary findings show that SARS-CoV-2-positive children faced elevated risk across a broad range of cardiovascular outcomes compared to controls. For the composite outcome of any cardiovascular event, RR was 1.63 in both CHD and non-CHD groups. Notable individual outcome RRs in the non-CHD group included myocarditis (RR 3.66; 95% CI 2.67–5.01), cardiogenic shock (RR 3.15; 95% CI 1.54–6.43), palpitations (RR 1.98; 95% CI 1.83–2.16), and chest pain (RR 1.84; 95% CI 1.75–1.92). In the CHD group, myocarditis showed RR 3.82 (95% CI 1.35–10.78), and atrial fibrillation — an abnormal heart rhythm — showed RR 2.64 (95% CI 1.15–6.05). Absolute risks were higher in CHD patients overall: 5.57% of SARS-CoV-2-positive CHD patients experienced any cardiovascular outcome, versus 2.19% of positive non-CHD patients.

Subgroup analyses revealed consistent elevated risks across age groups, sex, race/ethnicity, obesity status, COVID-19 severity, and dominant viral variants (pre-Delta, Delta, Omicron). Notably, elevated risk was also observed in children with no prior cardiovascular history, suggesting broad population-level impact. Sensitivity analyses — including exclusion of early pandemic cases, site-specific exclusions, and comparisons against influenza/RSV-infected controls — yielded consistent results.

Key limitations include potential misclassification of SARS-CoV-2 status (particularly given widespread at-home testing later in the pandemic), reliance on diagnostic codes without chart review, inability to account for reinfections, absence of family history data, and possible surveillance bias from differential healthcare utilization in the positive group. Generalizability beyond U.S. pediatric hospital networks warrants validation.

This study provides the largest and most comprehensive evidence to date on cardiovascular PASC in pediatric populations, extending prior adult-focused literature and filling a critical gap regarding CHD-stratified risk. The findings support proactive cardiovascular monitoring in children following SARS-CoV-2 infection, regardless of pre-existing cardiac status.

SARS-CoV-2 Infection Raises Cardiovascular Risk in Children, Including Those With Congenital Heart Defects

Philadelphia, PA — August 18, 2026

A large retrospective cohort study drawing on electronic health records from 19 U.S. children's hospitals found that children and adolescents infected with SARS-CoV-2 face a statistically significant elevated risk of a broad range of cardiovascular outcomes in the 28 to 179 days following infection, compared to uninfected controls. The study included 297,920 SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals and 915,402 SARS-CoV-2-negative controls, with findings that held consistently across patients both with and without congenital heart defects (CHDs) — structural abnormalities of the heart present from birth, and the most common congenital disorder in children.

Published in Nature Communications, the study leveraged data from the NIH-funded RECOVER (Researching COVID to Enhance Recovery) program, covering records from March 2020 through September 2023. Researchers used propensity score stratification to adjust for hundreds of measured confounders and estimated relative risk (RR) using a stratified modified Poisson regression model. Among children without CHDs, post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC) — defined here as health outcomes occurring 28 to 179 days after infection — included significantly elevated risks of myocarditis (inflammation of the heart muscle; RR 3.66, 95% CI 2.67–5.01), cardiogenic shock (RR 3.15, 95% CI 1.54–6.43), palpitations (RR 1.98, 95% CI 1.83–2.16), and chest pain (RR 1.84, 95% CI 1.75–1.92). Among children with CHDs, elevated risks were observed for myocarditis (RR 3.82, 95% CI 1.35–10.78), atrial fibrillation (an abnormal heart rhythm; RR 2.64, 95% CI 1.15–6.05), chest pain (RR 2.01, 95% CI 1.64–2.46), and heart failure (RR 1.77, 95% CI 1.48–2.10), among other outcomes. The composite risk of any cardiovascular outcome was elevated in both CHD patients (RR 1.63, 95% CI 1.47–1.80) and non-CHD patients (RR 1.63, 95% CI 1.57–1.69). Absolute risks also differed: 5.57% of SARS-CoV-2-positive patients with CHD experienced any post-acute cardiovascular outcome, compared to 4.00% of SARS-CoV-2-negative patients with CHD, while in the non-CHD group, the figures were 2.19% versus 1.26%, respectively.

The study's authors note that "children and adolescents with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection are at a statistically significant increased risk of various cardiovascular outcomes, including hypertension, ventricular arrhythmias, myocarditis, heart failure, cardiomyopathy, cardiac arrest, thromboembolism, chest pain, and palpitations, compared to uninfected controls." Subgroup analyses showed that elevated cardiovascular risk was consistent across age groups, sex, race and ethnicity, obesity status, COVID-19 severity, and dominant virus variant. Extensive sensitivity analyses — including negative control outcome experiments using 36 null-hypothesis outcomes, analyses restricted to patients without prior cardiovascular history, and comparisons across pandemic phases — supported the robustness of the primary findings.

The study was conducted within the RECOVER pediatric EHR cohort, a component of the NIH RECOVER Initiative, which draws on data from 19 U.S. children's hospitals and health institutions collectively covering more than 30 million patients under age 21, including more than 3 million individuals under 21 affected by COVID-19. Participating institutions span a mix of public and private healthcare systems and represent diverse racial, ethnic, socioeconomic, and geographic backgrounds across the United States. The study received support from the National Institutes of Health (OT2HL161847-01) and the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute (PCORI).

A new cohort study published in Nature Communications examined cardiovascular post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC — new or persistent health problems arising 28+ days after infection) in nearly 1.2 million children and adolescents. Drawing on EHR data from 19 U.S. children's hospitals within the NIH RECOVER consortium, the study compared 297,920 SARS-CoV-2-positive patients against 915,402 negative controls, with all individuals followed for at least six months.

Three findings stand out for researchers:

- Broad cardiovascular risk, not just rare events. Infected children showed significantly elevated risk across a wide range of outcomes — from myocarditis (RR 3.66 in those without congenital heart defects, or CHDs) to chest pain (RR 1.84) to hypertension (RR 1.47). These are not marginal signals.

- CHDs matter, but so does the absence of them. Children with CHDs — structural heart abnormalities present from birth — had higher absolute risks, but elevated relative risks were consistently observed in children without CHDs too, including those with no prior cardiovascular history.

- Propensity score stratification across hundreds of covariates, negative control experiments, and extensive subgroup analyses all supported the robustness of findings across age groups, sex, race/ethnicity, and dominant virus variants.

The study used ICD/SNOMED diagnostic codes without chart review, which introduces potential misclassification — a key limitation to weigh when interpreting effect sizes.

As pediatric PASC research matures, how should surveillance systems and health policy adapt to capture long-term cardiovascular burden in younger populations?

COVID-19 Isn't Just an Adult Problem: New Data Show Lasting Heart Risks in Children Too

When we think about long COVID and cardiovascular damage, the conversation has largely centered on adults. But a large new cohort study published in *Nature Communications* is shifting that focus — and the findings should prompt researchers and policymakers to take pediatric cardiovascular PASC (post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection) seriously.

## The Study at a Glance

Using electronic health records (EHR) from 19 U.S. children's hospitals and health systems within the NIH-funded RECOVER network, researchers tracked cardiovascular outcomes in children and adolescents (under age 21) between March 2020 and September 2023. The cohort included 297,920 SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals and 915,402 SARS-CoV-2-negative controls — making this one of the largest pediatric PASC studies to date. Every participant had at least six months of follow-up after cohort entry.

The primary analytical window was 28 to 179 days post-infection — a timeframe that captures the post-acute phase while remaining clinically meaningful for pediatric populations. To handle confounding from hundreds of measured covariates, the team used propensity score stratification, followed by stratified modified Poisson regression to estimate relative risks (RR).

A key design feature: all analyses were stratified by whether patients had a pre-existing congenital heart defect (CHD) — a structural heart abnormality present from birth, and the most common congenital disorder in children. This allowed the researchers to assess whether baseline cardiac vulnerability altered the PASC risk profile.

## What They Found

Across nearly every cardiovascular outcome examined, SARS-CoV-2-positive children fared worse than their uninfected counterparts. And the elevated risks were present in both the CHD and non-CHD groups.

For the composite outcome of "any cardiovascular event," infected children with CHD had an RR of 1.63 (95% CI: 1.47–1.80), identical to the point estimate in non-CHD children (RR: 1.63, 95% CI: 1.57–1.69). That symmetry is notable — it suggests the post-infection cardiovascular burden isn't confined to children already considered high-risk.

Looking at specific outcomes, myocarditis (inflammation of the heart muscle) stood out. In children without CHD, the RR for myocarditis was 3.66 (95% CI: 2.67–5.01); in those with CHD, it was 3.82 (95% CI: 1.35–10.78). Chest pain and palpitations — while more subjective — also showed substantial elevation. In non-CHD children, chest pain incidence was 1.23% among SARS-CoV-2-positive patients versus 0.61% in negative controls.

Heart failure, cardiomyopathy (disease of the heart muscle), ventricular arrhythmias (abnormal heart rhythms originating in the lower chambers), hypertension, thromboembolism, and cardiac arrest all showed statistically significant increases in at least one of the two subgroups.

## Who Is Most Affected?

The subgroup analyses revealed some important gradients. Adolescents over 12 and children aged 5–11 showed higher risks than the under-5 group. Patients with severe acute COVID-19 had higher composite cardiovascular risks than those with mild or asymptomatic infection. Non-Hispanic White patients showed the highest risks of any cardiovascular outcome, followed by Hispanic and Non-Hispanic Black groups — a pattern that warrants further investigation given the complex socioeconomic and biological factors at play.

Notably, even children with no prior cardiovascular history showed elevated post-infection risk, broadening the population of concern beyond those with obvious predisposing conditions.

## Methodological Strengths and Limitations Worth Knowing

The scale here is a genuine asset. With over 1.2 million total participants drawn from a geographically and demographically diverse network covering over 30 million pediatric patients across 41 states, this study has substantial power to detect even modest effect sizes.

The propensity score stratification approach — accommodating hundreds of covariates — is a meaningful improvement over traditional regression adjustment in this context. The team also ran negative control outcome experiments (using 36 outcomes where no true effect was expected) to calibrate residual bias from unmeasured confounders, and conducted extensive sensitivity analyses across pandemic phases, viral variants, and different population subsets. Results were consistent throughout.

That said, several limitations deserve attention. Control group misclassification is a real concern — particularly after 2021, when at-home testing became widespread and asymptomatic infections went largely unrecorded in EHRs. This would likely bias estimates toward the null, meaning true effect sizes may be larger than reported. Cardiovascular diagnoses relied on ICD and SNOMED codes without chart review, introducing potential outcome misclassification. Family history data were unavailable, and the analysis couldn't account for reinfection or vaccination during the study period.

## Why This Matters for the Research Community

The adult literature on cardiovascular PASC is substantial. This study provides the most comprehensive pediatric counterpart to date, and its consistent findings across subgroups — including children previously considered low-risk — have direct implications for surveillance, health system planning, and future research design.

For health policy researchers, the data make a case for dedicated post-COVID cardiovascular monitoring pathways in pediatric care. For methodologists, the study is a useful template for large-scale EHR-based PASC research with robust confounding control. And for epidemiologists studying long COVID, the CHD-stratified design highlights a model for incorporating pre-existing vulnerability into PASC analyses.

The bottom line: COVID-19 leaves cardiovascular footprints in children too — and those footprints are visible across the full spectrum of pediatric patients, regardless of prior heart health.
